articles.title: Show HN: SimDrop – Running iOS simulators in the macOS Finder sidebar
articles.summary:
Hi HN, I made a small macOS utility for my own iOS simulator workflow.
I kept running into two annoyances: getting config files in and out of a simulator is clunky (digging into CoreSimulator UUID folders or running simctl), and on the iPhone Duo simulator I couldn't even drag and drop images onto the window at all.
SimDrop puts every running iOS simulator in Finder's sidebar (under Locations) with two folders:
- Downloads/ (Files app > On My iPhone > Downloads)
- Photos and Videos/ (the simulator's Photos library)
Simulators appear when they boot and disappear when they shut down. Everything is also reachable from the terminal under ~/Library/CloudStorage/SimDrop-SimDrop/.
A couple of caveats up front:
- Dragging moves files by default (same as iCloud Drive, because it uses File Provider on the startup volume)—hold Option to copy.
- macOS 15+ and iOS simulators only (not physical devices).
It's free, open source (GPL-3.0), signed and notarized, and installable via Homebrew:
  brew install --cask rxliuli/tap/sim-drop

articles.title: ★ Obvious Affordances Are Due for a Comeback
articles.summary:
Speaking of Marcin Wichary, like me, he’s a big user of Apple Notes. Unlike me, he’s such a big user of Notes that he (somehow) uses Notes as the CMS for the whole Unsung blog. In a post this week, he wrote about how Notes — like file systems and most other notes apps — keeps two dates for each note: created and modified. You can sort your list of notes in Notes by either date; the default is by modification date, which Notes calls “edited”. Conveniently, Notes will remember your sorting preference on a per-folder basis. So if you have a folder of notes that you use as a journal, you can sort that folder by date created, without affecting the sort order for your other folders. (Notes only remembers each folder’s sort-by order per device, so if you use multiple devices, you’ll need to change the sort-by setting for a given folder on each device.)
In the editing view for a single note, however, Notes only shows one date, the modified/edited date, like so:
November 26, 2026 at 1:00 pm
Wichary writes:
This can feel frustrating. You know the data is there, you see it
in the left pane, part of the software recognizes and supports it,
but there seems to be no way to summon it in a place you want. I
looked through the context (right click) menus, and through the
main menu. I couldn’t find anything, and I assumed that
possibility just wasn’t there.
Then recently, years on, I accidentally clicked on the timestamp,
and this happened:
[Screen capture movie omitted.]
That click was what I needed all along. Clicking alternates
between “created” and “edited” timestamps. It even puts a little
prefix not just before the other date, but before both.
Yet… there is really no way to know this functionality is there.
Clicking the timestamp to toggle between the edited and created dates is a cool hidden feature. But as Wichary notes, why is it hidden?
I don’t necessarily mean that Notes had to do something like what
Finder or Bear do, and expose that data all the time — that kind
of stuff can feel heavy. But I think it’s important to make sure
all actions have their entry points somewhere where you can
discover them. Maybe it’s the main menu, maybe it’s the
right-click menu. I’m a fan of command palettes in part
because that’s where more esoteric options can go without
overloading other surfaces.
On the Mac, there probably ought to be an item in the View menu for this. But that wouldn’t help on iOS, which has no menu bar. The basic problem is that the timestamp at the top of every note is clickable, but it doesn’t look clickable. If clicking on something does something, that thing should look clickable. Just what “looking clickable” means is open for debate, but ought to be part of the standard visual language for the platform. It could look like a raised button. It could look like a recessed well. You could keep it flat and just draw a faint button shape behind the text. You could design something exuberantly fun, like making it look and animate like a train station split-flap display. You could be lazy and just underline the text — underlining, although gross, would at least be something. Things that are inert should look inert; things that are clickable should look clickable.1
This gets to the heart of the problem with Apple’s too-minimal UI language — and the rest of the industry mindlessly following Apple’s lead. There’s a wonderful rule of thumb oft attributed to Albert Einstein: Everything should be made as simple as possible, but not simpler. 
When clickable UI elements do not look clickable, they’ve been made too simple.
One More Thing
I long ago noticed, somehow, that the timestamps atop notes in Notes2 are clickable, to toggle between edited and created dates. But Wichary’s post brought to my attention a detail that I consider a violation of good design. When you first display a note, the timestamp at the top looks like this:
November 26, 2026 at 1:00 pm
That’s the edited date (which I really want to call “modified”) — but it doesn’t say so. It just shows the date. When you click it, it changes to:
Created: October 31, 2026 at 4:30 pm
Click again and you get:
Edited: November 26, 2026 at 1:00 pm
If you continue clicking, it keeps toggling between the timestamps with the “Created:” and “Edited:” prefix labels. The design violation I’m flagging is that the initial state doesn’t have a label, and there’s no way to get back to the initial unlabeled timestamp. If repeatedly clicking something cycles through multiple states, you should wind up exactly where you started. With these timestamps in Notes, the only way to get back to where you started — a timestamp with no label — is to close the note and reopen it. That’s clearly wrong.
This is a foul, not a bug. It’s a deliberate design decision. And I think we can presume how Apple arrived at this design. The solution I’d like to see is for the date to always be labeled — “Edited:” or “Created:”. Then clicking would just toggle between the two states. With two clicks, you’d be right back where you started. I think always showing these labels would also offer a gentle hint that you can click to change which date is shown. That’s not enough to fully suggest clickability, but it’d be better than nothing, which is what we have now. I’m guessing that the “simpler than possible” minimalist cohort at Apple complained that showing the “Edited:” label from the start is ugly clutter. So, we wound up with this unsatisfying compromise: no label at the start, but toggling between “Created:” and “Edited:” after you click on the timestamp.
Needless clutter ought to be omitted. Some elements are reasonably made optional. But when an item in an app has two timestamps associated with it, labeling which date is which isn’t clutter. Clarity is good. Eliminating ambiguity is good. Liking the way something looks should never come at the expense of conveying an understanding of how it works, or making it harder to use. If you’re not excited by the challenge of designing a presentation for the Notes timestamp that both looks good and suggests that it’s a clickable toggle, you are not a UI designer. You’re a graphic designer.
Dan Wineman wrote a good post on visual affordances back in 2013, just days after Apple unveiled iOS 7’s great flattening, which I’ll quote from again:
That’s what affordances do. They operate on the boundary between
sight and touch. You see a thing, often from a distance, and its
affordances give you enough information to simulate, in your mind,
the sensation of manipulating it. Unconsciously, you configure
your fine motor system in advance, so that by the time you get to
the door handle, your hand is already forming the right shape to
grasp it and pull the door open. [...]
Affordances are the baby to skeuomorphism’s bathwater. When they
engage our instincts just right, they create an emotional bond,
and the unfamiliar becomes inviting. Without them, it’s just
pictures under glass. It makes no difference how flat, how deep,
how minimal, or how ornate the look-and-feel is if it can’t show
us, when we look, how to feel.
This is the way back to the future. We don’t need to invent these designs. We just need to embrace again what we already know.
And things that could be clickable, but are disabled because of the current state of one or more conditions, should look clickable-but-disabled. Temporarily disabled is different from permanently inert, and that difference can and should be conveyed visually. ↩︎︎
I also noticed, long ago, that when the app is named Notes it’s often awkward to talk about notes in the app. Same for Reminders’ reminders, Files’ files, and, most ungainly of all, Shortcuts’ shortcuts. It’s like Abbott and Costello’s “Who’s on First” bit but less funny. What do you use for notes? Notes. That’s what I’m asking, where do you write them? Notes. Do you even keep notes? Absolutely. Where? Notes. Not what, where? Notes. I’ll kill you.
That said, my original idea for the name of what became Vesper was “What”, with slogans like, “You use What for your notes? Yes.” I still have the domain whatapp.net (which points nowhere). I had the idea before WhatsApp existed; by the time we started working on Vesper at the end of 2012, though, WhatsApp did exist, so the name What was out the door. That was probably for the best. ↩︎

articles.summary: Today's links Charles Koch is a cult leader: The "science of liberty" is no more scientific that Scientology. Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: Zune sucks; "Paintwork"; Wells Fargo claims forged signatures mean real binding arbitration; Corporate tax-breaks go to investors, not consumers; Anti-Lula conspirators eat each other; McKinsey created Big Pharma's price-gouging; Unions v two-tier contracts. Upcoming appearances: Virtual, Oxford, Santa Barbara, Montreal. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. Charles Koch is a cult leader (permalink) I've never met Charles Koch, but I sometimes feel like I know him, because he's such a type, instantly recognizable from his philosophy, actions, and pronouncements. Koch is clearly very smart, in the specific sense of sometimes being able to spot and act on true things that other people either can't see or can't bring themselves to pursue. When he inherited his father's fossil fuel empire, he made a series of investments in innovative processes that would substantially improve the efficiency of the operations, but would also take a very long time to pay off. These kinds of long-term capital investments are seriously out of fashion in big business, to the extent that the telecom giant Frontier walked away from a billion dollar ROI on fiber rollouts, because the payoff was a decade in the future, and influential market analysts were hostile to any company that made investments that took more than five years to pay off. Frontier executives' compensation was primarily stock-based, which means that those analysts could instantly make any executive who behaved in ways they disapproved of significantly poorer. So instead of pursuing long-term, substantial growth, Frontier chose short-term enshittification, for example by raising prices and cutting maintenance for over 1m customers who had no other ISPs to choose from. As a result, the company was forced to declare bankruptcy: https://pluralistic.net/2020/05/01/icann-can-and-did/#fiber-now This kind of story is why Koch is so openly hostile to the public markets, heaping scorn on founders who take their companies public. Koch was empirically right about how to run his father's business: a decade after he made those long-term investments the public markets wouldn't have tolerated, Koch Industries' profits had increased by 1,000%. Koch credits his extreme wealth and power to his superior intellect and temperament, boasting of his capacity for delayed gratification. This worship of patience and long-term consideration is a common theme among business leaders and people who venerate them as our civilization's natural and deserving autocrats. The veneration of a long-term outlook is at the heart of market fundamentalists' self-mythologizing as the keepers of "reason" and "rationalism." Anyone who sits below them on the social and economic hierarchy must be in thrall to their emotions, while those at the top of the system must have conquered their feelings (which facts famously don't care about!) so now they can see the world as it truly is. There's a whole body of pseudoscience, junk science, and debunked science they promote in support of this proposition. For example, these people love the "marshmallow test," in which children were left alone with a marshmallow and the promise of two marshmallows if they abstained from eating it. Long-term followups found a significant correlation between the children who abstained and long-term economic and professional success. But the marshmallow test is bunk. The kids who ate the marshmallow were overwhelmingly from poor and marginalized backgrounds and had long experience of adults promising them rewards that never materialized. They'd come to the entirely rational conclusion that if there's a chance to get a treat now, you should take it, rather than waiting for inconstant and unreliable authority figures to make good on their promises of jam tomorrow. Because those kids were poor and marginalized, they were more likely to face systemic discrimination and barriers in life, barriers that the wealthier, more privileged kids who held out for two marshmallows rarely encountered. Those wealthier kids were born on third base, so they scored more runs than the one-marshmallow kids who rarely got called out of the dugout. Far from proving that reason, self-denial and self-control are correlated with success, the experiment proved that rich people pass on their privilege to their offspring, who have an easier time in life no matter how defective their judgment and how error-prone their actions. Which is not to claim that there's no value in a long-term outlook. Charles Koch's long-range planning made Koch Industries far more profitable than its short-termist competitors. But Charles Koch is hardly a paragon of reason: perhaps more than anyone else in the world, he embodies Upton Sinclair's maxim that "It is difficult to get a man to understand something when his salary depends on his not understanding it." That's because Charles Koch, for all of his self-aggrandized long-termism, is one of the world's most ardent and important climate change deniers. Koch's intellectual contributions to climate denial are significant, but they're nothing compared to his financial contributions. There is no climate crackpot so unhinged, no junk science so flimsy, no conspiracy so absurd that Koch will not respond with showers of cash, buying their way into our discourse. This is motivated reasoning. After all, Koch owes his fortune, his power and his influence to burning fossil fuels. Moreover, he attributes that power and privilege to the market's infallible ability to elevate the wise and worthy. That's how he claims to be a champion of "personal liberty," despite his ability to decide how so many millions of the rest of us must live our lives. For Koch, the purpose of "liberty" is to allow each of us to audition in front of the market's self-regulating selection mechanism, so that the best among us (coolly rational and long-term in outlook) can be put in charge of the rest, in order to save them from their flawed emotionality and impulsivity. For Koch to acknowledge the obvious and worsening climate emergency would require him to shutter his coal plants: no one who believes in climate science could claim a "long-term" outlook while pumping gigatons of CO2 into the atmosphere. But even worse: acknowledging climate science means repudiating market orthodoxy. There is no greater indictment of the idea that allowing markets to self-regulate will lead to our collective prosperity than the climate emergency and the existential threat it represents to human civilization. Likewise, there is no greater indictment of markets' ability to select the wisest among us to rule over us than the fact that the market's chosen champions have committed themselves to driving our civilization, our species and the habitability of our planet over a cliff. Koch is a long-termist, but only when a long-term view serves his personal prejudices and privilege. The rest of the time, Koch breaks all speed records when he gobbles down that marshmallow. And because "the market" has given Koch so much power, he's eating all our marshmallows: https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-marshmallow-longtermism/ Koch is no rationalist. There is nothing more irrational than committing your fortune to destroying the civilization that it depends on. No one can lay claim to cool reason while they are busily sawing through the branch they're sitting on. I'm not claiming that any of the rest of us are any better. We are, all of us, inconstant in our rationality; we are all capable of self-deception and motivated reasoning. But most of us know it. We may not like being in a situation where other people can call us on our bullshit, but in our hearts of hearts, we know that we're better off for it: https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/09/impunitism/#rats-eating-my-face Koch is an engineer who exalts reason, but he can't distinguish between his beliefs and "science." When actual scientists perform careful experiments and analysis demonstrating that Koch needs to shut down his coal empire, his answers are, "Well that's your opinion" and "if you're so smart, why aren't you rich?" This inability to distinguish between your cherished delusions and objective reality is the most dangerous of all forms of emotion-driven self-sabotage. No one is more prone to this folly than the ultra-rich who have insulated themselves from consequences or even disagreement: https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/09/autocrats-of-trade-2/#witness-the-firepower-of-this-fully-armed-and-operational-battle-station Koch declares whatever he believes in to be "science." Take Koch's management philosophy, "Market Process Analysis," which he has declared to be a "science of liberty." Workers in Koch's empires are required to devote hours every week to studying this "science" and its precepts, despite the fact that his firms routinely ignore many of those tenets (such as "respect," the "ninth guiding principle" of Market Process Analysis). Writing for Jacobin, the labor historian Henry Snow breaks down the four unproven, self-serving ideological follies that make up this "science": https://jacobin.com/2026/11/koch-economics-workplace-tyranny-markets First: that "society" does not exist, and can only be understood as a collection of individuals. This "methodological individualism" is extremely convenient for the wealthy and powerful because their fortunes allow them to unilaterally wield enormous power over lots of other people. Meanwhile, the rest of us can only resist the demands that the rich make of us by wielding collective power, through unions, movements and democratic institutions. Koch's embrace of Thatcher's cheap quip about there being "no such thing as society" is great news for Koch, in other words, and (like so many of Thatcher's maxims) it is a demand dressed up as a truth. When Koch says "there is no such thing as society, only individuals," he means "you must not ever successfully resist my control by banding together – you must confine your resistance to acting as individuals, because that way you are doomed to fail." Koch's second principle is that individuals are only motivated by their self-interest ("psychological egoism"). This is likewise very convenient for someone whose power can only endure for so long as the rest of us can't work together to depose them. If Koch can convince you that your comrades and friends are actually only using you to better their own lot, then he can prevent you from making any kind of solidaristic sacrifice to help them (which guarantees that they'll never do the same for you). The third principle is a form of market fundamentalism: the belief that at a societal level, plans can't ever work, that the only way to steer society is through "self-correcting" markets. Here's another self-serving, convenient rationalization: if the market leaves Koch rich and you poor; if it leaves him comfortable and you struggling; that's just how it is. If you were to band together to create democratic institutions that tried to build a fairer, better society, you would be doomed to fail, because your planning system could never "incorporate as much information" as the market, which is the world's greatest computer and integrator of "signals" that lead to the most efficient allocation and production possible. The fourth principle is more market fundamentalism: the belief that "everything is – and should be – a market." In a world of individuals who can only behave selfishly, where all grand plans are doomed to fail, the only way to improve the world and our lot in it is to "create incentives" and "design mechanisms" that let the market make its magic. As Snow writes, people who espouse these beliefs follow Koch's lead in describing them as "scientific truths," while downgrading every disagreement to mere "ideology." They claim to be moved by facts, while their fuzzy-headed opponents are moved by feelings. These people are part of a long lineage of "scientific managers" who have come up with doctrines and methods that are sold as ways to improve production and make us all better off, but always turn out to be ways for bosses to atomize, demoralize and control their workers: https://pluralistic.net/2021/02/24/gwb-rumsfeld-monsters/#bossware Inevitably, these "scientists" claim to have discovered a freestanding and objective "human nature." But scholars who subject the idea of "human nature" to scientific and historical scrutiny have repeatedly and reliably discovered a wide spectrum of human natures, which are not fixed from birth, but are rather determined by a mix of temperament, societal norms and material reality: https://pluralistic.net/2022/03/08/three-freedoms/#anti-fatalism Koch isn't describing the world as it is, he's describing the world as he wishes it was, because that way his wealth and power would be both justified and eternal. Like I say, this is an extremely recognizable type of guy, the kind of person who insists that their preferences are scientific truths. articles.title: Protect Your Web Forms Against Spam Bots
articles.summary:
The comments form that appears at the bottom of every article in this blog is under constant abuse by spam bots. I added a CAPTCHA to it a few years ago and at the time it seemed to help some, but spammers have now figured out how to bypass them. As a result, my comments inbox has been getting out of control lately.
In this article I'm going to share a solution that I built to help me reduce spam on this blog from 30-40 messages per day to just about 2-3 per month. It is based on the "proof of work" concept, and unlike CAPTCHAs, it does not rely on third-party services. It is also better for users, because it does not require them to solve silly puzzles or even know that they are being verified. I have implemented the solution in Python and Flask, because that is what this blog runs on, but once you understand how it works you should have no trouble porting it to other languages or frameworks.

A pair of Chinese firms installed Nvidia Corp.’s powerful
Blackwell semiconductors in a Shanghai data center linked to Alice
Huang, the woman at the heart of a controversy surrounding the US
chipmaker.
The gear installed at the Yangtze River Delta Project included a
GB300 NVL72 rack, among Nvidia’s most powerful products, according
to a serial number specified in documents submitted to Chinese
regulators in November. Shanghai Shuoyao offered the hardware as
collateral to obtain a 96 million yuan ($14 million) loan from
Shanghai Innovation Bank, according to filings from the lender
that were reviewed by Bloomberg News.
A second firm, Shanghai Kezhan, controlled by a Tokyo-based
parent, described a GB200 server — which also relies on Blackwell
chips — at the facility. That description was provided in
documents when it obtained a 90 million yuan loan in late 2025
from a finance-leasing firm wholly owned by a local Shanghai
government agency. [...]
The submissions reveal for the first time that Nvidia’s Blackwell
processors found their way into a Chinese data center that has
ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed. These processors were until
recently Nvidia’s most powerful data center products, and they’ve
always been illegal to ship to China without a US license.

articles.title: Show HN: DragDropMath – Learn math by feel
articles.summary:
Hi HN!
I am a professional physicist and I shuffle symbols in equations and mathematical expressions all day long. During my PhD (almost 20 years ago) I noticed that it is as if the symbols have their own 'physics', which makes the wrong moves impossible and the right ones obvious.
So I created DragDropMath, where you can learn how to simplify mathematical expressions and how to solve equations by dragging symbols around, and only correct moves are allowed, so you get to feel what's right without experiencing (and so learning) wrong moves.
I always wanted to make this, but life got in the way. Then a few weeks ago I saw declarative dragging (https://declarative-dragging.github.io/) on the front page of HN and the spark came back!
It took quite a few rounds to get the feel right, but I think it's close to what happens in my mind when I mentally manipulate these expressions.
A few more points:
- There are no ads, no trackers, no accounts (it's a static website and progress is saved in the browser cache).
- Teachers can create their own problem sets, encoded in the link.
- I plan to add more chapters (trigonometry, complex numbers, some calculus) but I first need to figure out the 'right' mode of interaction.
- I just started working on the experience from mobile, so there may still be some rough edges there
I'm curious to know what you think, if you have suggestions for content, if you spot anything that I should fix, if you have feature requests! Thank you in advance

articles.title: Pluralistic: Taylorism and AI's shared sales-pitch (27 Nov 2026)
articles.summary: Today's links Taylorism and AI's shared sales-pitch: Bosses will buy anything if they think it'll give them more control over their workers. Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: UK recordings copyright won't go to 95 years; McDonald's sandwich patent; McLaren's son torches punk tat; Chestburster turkey; O(N^2) nationalism. Upcoming appearances: Virtual, Oxford, Santa Barbara, Montreal. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. Taylorism and AI's shared sales-pitch (permalink) More than a century ago, the most powerful, wealthiest men in the world fell for a con-artist named Frederick Winslow Taylor, who sold them expensive consulting services to help them apply "Scientific Management" to their companies: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Winslow_Taylor Upon receipt of eye-popping consulting fees, Taylor dispatched unqualified young men in "scientist" drag (lab coats, clipboards, stopwatches) to fan out over factory floors. These smart young men noted how much time each worker at each station took to perform each task, then "optimized" each worker using a homebrew choreographer's notation that showed the "correct" way to make each motion and set an upper bound for how many seconds it should take to perform each task. Notably, these "scientists" refused to discuss their findings with the workers they observed: they never asked why a worker made a specific motion or tackled a task in a certain way. The workers were presumed to be ploddingly unreflective about their jobs (at best), or malicious featherbedders who were stealing from the boss by slacking off (at worst). Either way, Taylor's "scientists" could see no reason to discuss their findings with the workers. The job of the "scientists" was to transform those workers into a well-oiled machine, and no one but a blockhead would ask a piston or a gear why it chose to move the way it did. To use a technical term, these "scientists" were fucking idiots and their recommendations were (to use another technical term) bullshit. Not only did they set impossible quotas for workers, they were also notably bad at choreography and routinely required workers to move in ways that resulted in early fatigue and high rates of injury. Wherever Taylor's "scientists" went, morale plunged, labor unrest surged, and the business was made worse off. Which all raises a question: why would the owners of these businesses – who had the intelligence and self-interest to build up extremely profitable enterprises – throw away their money and kneecap their firms on this charlatanry? The answer lies in the psychology of Taylor's sales-pitch. Taylor's marks owed their fortunes and power to their ability to scale up their firms to sizes never before seen, thanks to innovations like the assembly line and to exogenous factors like mechanized transportation and long-distance telecommunications, which let them address much larger markets than their predecessors. The downside to this was a large workforce (too large to keep individual tabs on) that was spread out over a large factory floor or complex (too large to constantly observe). This created a paradox: these powerful, wealthy men were vulnerable to the lowest footsoldiers in their laboring armies, any of whom might slack off, organize a union or sabotage the line, safe in the knowledge that they were part of a vast cohort that could neither be tractably surveilled nor controlled. Imagine the indignation those industrial titans must have experienced at the thought that some mere pismire could blacken their eyes and destroy their profits, and nothing could be done about it! After all, the quest for wealth and power is, above everything else, the quest for impunity, for an existence in which you can never be thwarted: https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/09/impunitism/#rats-eating-my-face The Robber Barons' fury at this indignity made them easy marks for Taylor's salesmen, who promised them a return to the natural order in which workers would be literally reduced to machine-parts. After Taylor's men had done their jobs, the boss could strut the catwalks high above the factory floor and observe a visibly cowed workforce, where every worker's every moment was a constant reminder that they were there to do as they were told, not to exercise judgment, air grievances, or act in their own self-interest. Like every power-tripping control freak, these business tyrants were their own worst enemies, doomed to a long and humiliating Tarkin's Downfall ("The more you tighten your grip, Tarkin, the more star systems will slip through your fingers" – P.L. Organa). Taylor was no master of improving industrial production, but he was a genius at figuring out how to sell things to anxious bosses. I don't know whether Taylor believed his nonsense: he might have been every bit as satisfied as his marks at the sight of a factory full of human workers who'd been reduced to the state of machine-parts. Perhaps he truly had no inkling that the reason his services sold so well is that they played perfectly on the insecurities of business tyrants. Or maybe he was a cynic with a thorough grasp of oligarch psychology and a total indifference to the quality of workers' lives and the long-term health of his customers' business interests. Perhaps some of Taylor's executives were true believers, while others were cynics, and together they formed an unbeatable partnership because the former would go where the latter would not (and vice versa): https://pluralistic.net/2026/07/24/supplemental-income/#andrew-tate-gwyneth-paltrow It doesn't matter. The purpose of a system is what it does. Taylor created a template for selling garbage products to insecure bosses that made workers' lives worse and undermined the health of the firm, and that template has been mobilized by firms large and small in the years since. Every bossware company that made bank selling companies surveillance tools during the pandemic's work-from-home phase wasn't just doing Taylorism(1) (timing, surveilling and scoring workers), but also Taylorism(2) (fleecing bosses who were terrified of their workforce's power and independence): https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/02/despotism-on-demand/#virtual-whips (In case you have any doubt, yes, this is a post about AI.) Many workers – and even managers – have expressed bafflement at their bosses' love-affairs with AI. Even workers who can see ways to use AI tools to improve their jobs around the margins are shocked (and sometimes resentful) at their bosses' insistence that they use AI for everything, even when that adds expense and reduces quality: https://pluralistic.net/2026/08/01/dare-snot/#i-will-fucking-piledrive-you-if-you-mention-ai-again At the heart of this confusion is the fact that these same bosses are usually unwavering when it comes to measuring profit and loss and requiring a solid business-case for major shifts in corporate organization. Despite this, an AI pitchman can send these bosses swooning with all the ardor of Jensen Huang meeting an attractive woman who flirtatiously asks him to take her on a "quirky" date, say, to one of his chip warehouses? Bosses are such easy marks for AI pitchmen for the same reason their predecessors were easy marks for Taylor's salesforce. The modern boss is a financial engineer, possibly with a law degree, whose main expertise is in balance-sheet manipulation and shareholder relations. These bosses don't know how to do anything. They can come up with as many amazing plans to revolutionize their businesses as they want, but inevitably, those plans lead to ego-shattering confrontations with skilled workers who tell them that all their ideas are impossible, illegal, or stupid: https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/05/fisher-price-steering-wheel/#billionaire-solipsism Enter the AI salesman, offering the prospect of a new workforce of literal mechanical slaves, whose presence allows the boss to fire 90% of their workers, with the result that the remaining workers will be so terrorized at the thought of losing their jobs that they never even think of sassing back: https://pluralistic.net/2026/07/10/posthuman-as-in-no-humans/#hell-is-other-people This won't work. Replacing workers with chatbots is as counterproductive as putting one of Taylor's choreographers in charge of them. Sure, AI can help workers: if the workers get to decide how the chatbots are integrated into their jobs, and if this integration doesn't increase the pace of work, making it impossible for the human workers to catch the machine's mistakes: https://pluralistic.net/2025/12/05/pop-that-bubble/#u-washington After all, the statistical methods used to produce AI outputs produce errors that are as close to being correct as is statistically possible, while still being wrong: https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/06/nonfungible/#theory-free Ergonomics are real. Taylorism is fake. Automation is real. AI is fake: https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/12/god-in-the-box/#llms-are-fake Statistical extrapolation tools can lead to productivity gains – just as incorporating ergonomic principles into the design of the job-site can improve productivity and reduce injury. But in both cases, the gains are contingent on the workers having a say in the deployment and a veto over demands that don't work for them. But that's not how you sell Taylorism…or AI. The pitch isn't about making the business more profitable or efficient. Such a proposition has limited efficacy and competes against other forms of capital investment that might be better for the bottom line. The pitch is about easing the psychological trauma of being the boss but not being able to boss people around. That's an unbeatable proposition. No one will ever lose money by betting on the insecurities of America's business tyrants.
